question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man is seen this afternoon in the ambulatory orthopedic suite immediately before a planned right knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy that the surgeon estimates will last under one hour under general anesthesia with a same-day discharge. He drove himself to the hospital, parked on the third deck of the garage, and walked briskly through the corridor without shortness of breath or assistance, stating that he still manages a daily two-mile neighborhood walk despite intermittent knee catching. His baseline activity is otherwise unrestricted; he mows his lawn, lifts groceries, and climbs the single flight of stairs to his bedroom several times a day. The knee problem developed after a low-energy twist six months ago and has been treated conservatively with physical therapy and NSAIDs; he has not required crutches, braces, off-loading boots, or any form of immobilization. Review of recent medical events confirms that he has not undergone any procedure, endoscopy, or hospitalization in the preceding four weeks, and the electronic record contains no admissions for systemic infection, chest infiltrate, or heart-failure decompensation during that period. His past medical history is notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease related to a 40-pack-year cigarette exposure; he quit seven years ago and now uses tiotropium once daily and an albuterol metered-dose inhaler about twice a week before yard work, with no emergency-department visits or steroid tapers in the last year. Ten years earlier, after a transatlantic flight, he developed aching in the left calf and was found on duplex ultrasonography to have an occlusive thrombus in the popliteal and proximal posterior tibial veins; he completed a six-month course of warfarin with complete symptom resolution and has remained off anticoagulation since. He has never experienced sudden pleuritic chest pain or shortness of breath that prompted imaging for embolism, and surveillance CT scans performed for unrelated reasons have been devoid of pulmonary artery filling defects. There is no personal history of malignancy, myocardial infarction, stroke, inflammatory bowel disease, connective-tissue disorder, or hereditary bleeding or clotting syndromes, and he denies that any first-degree relative has suffered an unprovoked clot or been told of an inherited thrombophilia. Medications taken this morning include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled, lisinopril 10 mg daily for well-controlled hypertension, and a single 81 mg aspirin tablet, which he stopped two days ago per pre-operative instructions; he does not use hormone preparations, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs other than the aspirin. He drinks one beer with dinner on weekends, denies illicit substance use, and maintains a body mass index of 28 kg/m². On examination he sits comfortably on the gurney, conversing in full sentences. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago show temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 80 beats·min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, intact dentition, and full neck extension. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated; S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung fields are clear to auscultation with faint end-expiratory wheeze that resolves after coached exhalation and no crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Inspection of the lower extremities shows serpiginous, thin-walled superficial veins coursing up the medial aspects of both calves that become more prominent when he stands; the skin is warm, of equal color bilaterally, and free of edema or palpable cords, and calf circumferences measured 15 cm below the tibial tuberosity are symmetric. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are bounding and equal. Neurologic screening demonstrates full orientation and 5/5 strength throughout except for painful inhibition with resisted right knee flexion; sensation is intact. Only a single 20-gauge peripheral IV placed in the left forearm is present; he has never had a tunneled catheter, implanted port, or peripherally inserted central line. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn earlier today reveal hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, hematocrit 45 %, platelets 250 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.0 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 78 beats·min⁻¹ with no ST-segment changes, and a portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained for COPD surveillance last month demonstrates hyperinflated lungs without focal infiltrate, mass, or cardiomegaly. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided ninety minutes ago, and sequential calf compressors are at the bedside awaiting placement after induction; no pharmacologic prophylaxis has yet been administered while the anesthesia team finalizes the plan for laryngeal mask airway and multimodal analgesia.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds weighted patient and procedural risk factors:
- Age 62 (61–74 years): 2.
- Planned arthroscopic knee surgery: 2. Count the procedure once; this is not knee replacement.
- Prior duplex-confirmed DVT: 3, even though it was remote and provoked.
- BMI 28 kg/m² (>25): 1.
- Visible varicose veins in both calves: 1 total.
- COPD: 1.
No additional points are supported for immobility, swollen legs, current fracture, malignancy, thrombophilia, or central venous access. The forearm IV is peripheral.
Total = 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10.
Final answer: 10
